description: We are high school students from Fortaleza with experience in physics, programming, AI, and scientific olympiads. For the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge, we want to use real lunar and astronomical data to build a simple tool for comparing landing sites and mission dates. We are looking for teammates with experience in astronomy, data analysis, visualization, or design.
summary: Landing Guide helps students and the public explore two essential questions about a lunar location and time: can sunlight reach it, and is Earth visible for direct communication? Users choose a point on a 3D Moon, select a UTC date, and receive short explanations of the modeled conditions. The application combines NASA LRO/LOLA terrain data with precomputed Sun and Earth positions for ten south-pole locations. Other coordinates receive a clearly labeled geometry-only approximation. Optional comparisons and time charts reveal how conditions change. By making NASA data easier to explore, Landing Guide helps people understand the trade-offs between location, timing, potential solar energy, and communication. Sunlight does not guarantee electrical output, and Earth visibility does not guarantee a working radio link.
details:
Near the Moon's south pole, a low Sun and crater walls can create different conditions on a ridge and a nearby floor. Landing Guide lets people explore when sunlight reaches a location and how Earth clears its local skyline.

Choose directly on the 3D Moon, use a standard list, or enter coordinates. The Explorer shows the 3D Moon around the south pole. Sunlight and Earth visibility are explained in Conditions, rather than represented as objects beside the globe. Rendered relief is visual context. Open Conditions for the modeled local-visibility results and short energy and communication explanations.

Catalogued sites offer optional time charts and a data table. Users can compare places at the same UTC and share the active scenario, including its assumptions. An optional Moon walk explores an illustrative base. Its terrain, buildings, lighting and Earth appearance do not feed the visibility calculations.

The catalogue covers ten south-pole locations, with 721 hourly samples from November 15 to December 15, 2026: 30 elapsed days. Its offline pipeline uses LRO/LOLA elevation data for sampled terrain horizons and NAIF SPICE kernels for Sun/Earth sky positions. The browser reads saved results. For example, the Shackleton-de Gerlache connecting ridge has modeled sunlight on November 15 and November 22 at 00:00 UTC, while Earth changes from hidden to entirely above the modeled skyline.

At catalogued sites, solar visibility approximates a uniform disk against the skyline at its central azimuth. The default Earth rule requires the whole disk to clear the skyline. Other coordinates use approximate directions on a reference sphere, without local terrain obstruction. The interface labels this distinction. Atlas loading includes a cached background worker and fallbacks; the viewport includes graphics-recovery handling. No device-performance benchmark is claimed.

Landing Guide is educational. Rendered relief is separate from the horizon calculation. Sunlight does not guarantee panel output; Earth in view does not establish ground-station access or a working radio link. Hourly samples do not resolve exact rise/set times. An archived JPL Horizons comparison covers 16 epochs at one location, not all terrain or engineering results. The app does not certify landing safety or provide an operational mission plan.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Three.js and Vite. The offline science pipeline uses Python, NumPy, SpiceyPy and Skyfield, with JSON Schema validation. Project code is MIT licensed; third-party resources keep their own terms and credits.

OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code assisted with development, repository research, documentation, and preparation of the script and presentation. No AI-generated images were created for this project. AI tools are not the source of the astronomical or terrain data; those inputs and the model limitations are identified separately.
